# Common x86-64 Instructions {#appendix-b-common-x86-instructions}

Reading the Tables {#reading-the-tables}
------------------

The tables of instructions presented in this appendix include:

-   The instruction code.

-   The operands used.

-   The flags used.

-   A brief description of what the instruction does.

In the operands section, it will list the type of operands it takes. If
it takes more than one operand, each operand will be separated by a
comma. Each operand will have a list of codes which tell whether the
operand can be an immediate-mode value (I), a register (R), or a memory
address (M). For example, the `movq` instruction is listed as
`I/R/M, R/M`. This means that the first operand can be any kind of
value, while the second operand must be a register or memory location.
Note, however, that in x86-64 assembly language you cannot have more
than one operand be a memory location. In the floating-point table, X
is an _%xmm_ register.

Most instructions come in several sizes, with the suffix `b` (1 byte),
`w` (2 bytes), `l` (4 bytes) or `q` (8 bytes); the tables show the `q`
form, the normal size in this book. Remember that writing a 32-bit
register (`l`) also clears the upper 32 bits of its 64-bit register,
while `b` and `w` leave them alone (see Chapter 10).

In the flags section, it lists the flags in the _%rflags_
register affected by the instruction (\"none\" if it doesn\'t change
any, and \"undefined\" if it leaves them with meaningless values). The
following flags are mentioned:

O:

:   Overflow flag. This is set to true if the destination
    operand was not large enough to hold the result of the instruction.

S:

:   Sign flag. This is set to the sign of the last result.

Z:

:   Zero flag. This flag is set to true if the result of the
    instruction is zero.

A:

:   Auxiliary carry flag. This flag is set for
    carries and borrows between the third and fourth bit. It is not
    often used.

P:

:   Parity flag. This flag is set to true if the low byte of
    the last result had an even number of 1 bits.

C:

:   Carry flag. Used in arithmetic to say whether or not the
    result should be carried over to an additional byte. If the carry
    flag is set, that usually means that the destination register could
    not hold the full result. It is up to the programmer to decide on
    what action to take (i.e. - propagate the result to another byte,
    signal an error, or ignore it entirely).

Other flags exist, but they are much less important.
[Appendix L](appendix-l-registers-and-flags.qmd#appendix-l-registers-and-flags)
lists every bit of _%rflags_ and the flags that each conditional jump
tests.

Data Transfer Instructions {#data-transfer-instructions}
--------------------------

These instructions perform little, if any computation. Instead they are
mostly used for moving data from one place to another. None of them
changes the flags.

Table B-1. Data Transfer Instructions.

**Instruction** _Operands_ -----> Affected Flags.

---

**movq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> none:

> This copies a quadword (8 bytes) of data from one location to
  another. `movq %rax, %rbx` copies the contents of _%rax_ to _%rbx_.
  `movl` copies 4 bytes (and, if the destination is a register, sets
  the upper 32 bits of its 64-bit register to 0), `movw` 2 bytes and
  `movb` 1 byte. When the destination is memory, an immediate value
  must fit in 32 bits (it is sign-extended to 64); into a register, the
  assembler uses a longer form, `movabsq`, for bigger numbers.

**movzbq**, **movzwq** _R/M_, _R_ -----> none:

> Copy a byte or a 2-byte word into a 64-bit register, filling the rest
  with zeros (*zero extension*, for unsigned values). `movzbq (%rdi),
  %rcx` reads one character. There is no `movzlq`: `movl` already
  clears the upper half.

**movsbq**, **movswq**, **movslq** _R/M_, _R_ -----> none:

> Copy a byte, a 2-byte word or a 4-byte doubleword into a 64-bit
  register with *sign extension*, for signed values.

**cmovcc** _R/M_, _R_ -----> none:

> Conditional move: copies the first operand to the second only if the
  condition `cc` is true (the same conditions as the conditional jumps
  below, for example `cmovgq`). Compilers use it instead of a jump
  around a `mov`.

**leaq** _M_, _R_ -----> none:

> This takes a memory location given in the standard format, and,
  instead of loading the contents of the memory location, loads the
  computed address. For example, `leaq 5(%rbp,%rcx,1), %rax` loads the
  address computed by `5 + %rbp + 1*%rcx` and stores that in _%rax_,
  and `leaq data(%rip), %rbx` loads the address of `data`. It is also
  used to add numbers: `leaq 15(%rdi), %rdx` computes `%rdi + 15`.

**popq** _R/M_ -----> none:

> Pops the top of the stack into the given location. This is equivalent
  to performing `movq (%rsp), R/M` followed by `addq $8, %rsp`. `popfq`
  is a variant which pops the top of the stack into the _%rflags_
  register (and so changes all the flags).

**pushq** _I/R/M_ -----> none:

> Pushes the given value onto the stack. This is the equivalent to
  performing `subq $8, %rsp` followed by `movq I/R/M, (%rsp)`. `pushfq`
  is a variant which pushes the current contents of the _%rflags_
  register onto the top of the stack.

**xchgq** _R/M_, _R/M_ -----> none:

> Exchange the values of the given operands. With a memory operand it
  is *atomic* (see `lock` in the integer instructions).

**bswapq** _R_ -----> none:

> Reverses the order of the 8 bytes of a register: `0x0102030405060708`
  becomes `0x0807060504030201`. It converts between the little-endian
  order of x86-64 and the big-endian order of network protocols (see
  [Order of Bytes in a Word](10-counting-like-a-computer.qmd#order-of-bytes-in-a-word)).

**cltq** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Sign-extends _%eax_ into _%rax_, like `movslq %eax, %rax` but one
  byte shorter. Intel calls it `cdqe`.

**setcc** _R/M_ -----> none:

> Sets a byte to 1 if the condition `cc` is true and to 0 if it is not
  (the same conditions as the conditional jumps, for example `setl`).
  Follow it with `movzbq` to get a 64-bit 0 or 1:
  `cmpq %rsi, %rdi; setl %al; movzbq %al, %rax`.

---

Integer Instructions {#integer-instructions}
--------------------

These are basic calculating instructions that operate on signed or
unsigned integers. They are shown with the `q` suffix; the `l`, `w` and
`b` forms work on 4, 2 and 1 bytes.

Table B-2. Integer Instructions.

**Instruction** _Operands_ -----> Affected Flags.

---

**adcq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Add with carry. Adds the carry bit and the first operand to the
  second, and, if there is an overflow, sets overflow and carry to
  true. This is usually used for operations larger than a register. The
  addition on the least-significant quadword would take place using
  `addq`, while additions to the other quadwords would use the `adcq`
  instruction to take the carry from the previous add into account. For
  the usual case, this is not used, and `addq` is used instead.

**addq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Addition. Adds the first operand to the second, storing the result in
  the second. If the result is larger than the destination register,
  the overflow and carry bits are set to true. This instruction
  operates on both signed and unsigned integers.

**cqto** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Converts the quadword in _%rax_ into the octoword (16 bytes)
  consisting of _%rdx_:_%rax_ with sign extension: _%rdx_ becomes all
  zeros or all ones. This is used before issuing an `idivq` instruction.
  Intel calls it `cqo`. `cltq` (`cdqe` for Intel) sign-extends _%eax_
  into _%rax_.

**cmpq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Compares two integers. It does this by subtracting the first operand
  from the second. It discards the results, but sets the flags
  accordingly. Usually used before a conditional jump.

**decq** _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P:

> Decrements the register or memory location. Use `decb` to decrement a
  byte instead of a quadword. It doesn\'t change the carry flag.

**divq** _R/M_ -----> undefined:

> Performs unsigned division. Divides the 128-bit number contained in
  the combined _%rdx_:_%rax_ registers by the value in the register or
  memory location specified. The _%rax_ register contains the resulting
  quotient, and the _%rdx_ register contains the resulting remainder.
  If the quotient is too large to fit in _%rax_, or the divisor is 0, it
  triggers a divide error (Linux sends the signal `SIGFPE`). Set _%rdx_
  to 0 first to divide the 64-bit number in _%rax_.

**idivq** _R/M_ -----> undefined:

> Performs signed division. Operates just like `divq` above; use `cqto`
  first to divide the 64-bit number in _%rax_.

**imulq** _I/R/M_, _R_ -----> O/C:

> Performs signed multiplication and stores the result in the second
  operand. With three operands, `imulq $10, %rax, %rbx` multiplies the
  second by the first and stores the result in the third. With a single
  operand, it multiplies _%rax_ by it, and the full 128-bit result is
  stored in _%rdx_:_%rax_. The overflow and carry flags say whether the
  result didn\'t fit.

**incq** _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P:

> Increments the given register or memory location. Use `incb` to
  increment a byte instead of a quadword. It doesn\'t change the carry
  flag.

**mulq** _R/M_ -----> O/C:

> Perform unsigned multiplication of _%rax_ by the operand, with the
  128-bit result in _%rdx_:_%rax_.

**negq** _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Negates (gives the two\'s complement inversion of) the given register
  or memory location.

**sbbq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Subtract with borrowing. This is used in the same way that `adcq` is,
  except for subtraction. Normally only `subq` is used.

**subq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Subtract the two operands. This subtracts the first operand from the
  second, and stores the result in the second operand. This instruction
  can be used on both signed and unsigned numbers.

**xaddq** _R_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Exchange and add: the second operand gets the sum of both, and the
  first operand gets the old value of the second. With the `lock`
  prefix, `lock xaddq %rax, counter(%rip)` adds to a counter shared by
  several threads and returns its old value, as one indivisible step.

**cmpxchgq** _R_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Compare and exchange: compares _%rax_ with the second operand. If
  they are equal, it sets the zero flag and stores the first operand in
  the second; if not, it clears the zero flag and loads the second
  operand into _%rax_. With `lock`, it is the basis of locks and other
  structures shared by threads.

**lock** _prefix_ -----> none:

> Makes the instruction that follows (an `add`, `sub`, `inc`, `dec`,
  `and`, `or`, `xor`, `xadd`, `cmpxchg`, `bts`, `btr` or `btc` on
  memory) one
  indivisible operation, so that no other processor core sees or
  changes the memory in the middle of it.

---

Logic Instructions {#logic-instructions}
------------------

These instructions operate on memory as bits instead of numbers.

Table B-3. Logic Instructions.

**Instruction** _Operands_ -----> Affected Flags.

---

**andq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Performs a logical and of the contents of the two operands, and
  stores the result in the second operand. Sets the overflow and carry
  flags to false.

**notq** _R/M_ -----> none:

> Performs a logical not on each bit in the operand. Also known as a
  one\'s complement.

**orq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Performs a logical or between the two operands, and stores the result
  in the second operand. Sets the overflow and carry flags to false.

**popcntq** _R/M_, _R_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Counts the bits set to 1 in the first operand and stores the number in
  the second. Not every old processor has it.

**rclq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/C:

> Rotates the given location\'s bits to the left the number of times in
  the first operand, which is either an immediate-mode value or the
  register _%cl_. The carry flag is included in the rotation, making it
  use 65 bits instead of 64. Also sets the overflow flag.

**rcrq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/C:

> Same as above, but rotates right.

**rolq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/C:

> Rotate bits to the left. It sets the overflow and carry flags, but
  does not count the carry flag as part of the rotation. The number of
  bits to roll is either specified in immediate mode or is contained in
  the _%cl_ register.

**rorq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/C:

> Same as above, but rotates right.

**salq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Arithmetic shift left. The sign bit is shifted out to the carry flag,
  and a zero bit is placed in the least significant bit. Other bits are
  simply shifted to the left. This is the same as the regular shift
  left. The number of bits to shift is either specified in immediate
  mode or is contained in the _%cl_ register.

**sarq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Arithmetic shift right. The least significant bit is shifted out to
  the carry flag. The sign bit is shifted in, and kept as the sign bit.
  Other bits are simply shifted to the right. The number of bits to
  shift is either specified in immediate mode or is contained in the
  _%cl_ register.

**shlq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Logical shift left. This shifts all bits to the left (sign bit is not
  treated specially). The leftmost bit is pushed to the carry flag. The
  number of bits to shift is either specified in immediate mode or is
  contained in the _%cl_ register.

**shrq** _I/cl_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Logical shift right. This shifts all bits in the register to the
  right (sign bit is not treated specially). The rightmost bit is
  pushed to the carry flag. The number of bits to shift is either
  specified in immediate mode or is contained in the _%cl_ register.

**testq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Does a logical and of both operands and discards the results, but
  sets the flags accordingly. `testq %rax, %rax` is a common way to
  compare _%rax_ with 0.

**xorq** _I/R/M_, _R/M_ -----> O/S/Z/P/C:

> Does an exclusive or on the two operands, and stores the result in
  the second operand. Sets the overflow and carry flags to false.
  `xorl %eax, %eax` is the usual way to set _%rax_ to 0.

**btq** _I/R_, _R/M_ -----> C:

> Bit test: copies the bit of the second operand whose number is the
  first operand into the carry flag; `btq $2, %rax` followed by `jc`
  jumps if bit 2 of _%rax_ is 1. `btsq`, `btrq` and `btcq` also set the
  bit to 1, reset it to 0 or complement it. The zero flag doesn\'t
  change; the other flags are undefined.

**bsfq**, **bsrq** _R/M_, _R_ -----> Z:

> Bit scan forward and reverse: the number of the lowest (`bsf`) or the
  highest (`bsr`) bit that is 1 in the first operand goes to the second.
  For `0x50` (`0101 0000`) they give 4 and 6. If the first operand is 0
  they set the zero flag and the result is undefined; the other flags
  are undefined.

**tzcntq**, **lzcntq** _R/M_, _R_ -----> Z/C:

> Count the trailing (lowest) or leading (highest) zero bits. Unlike
  `bsf` and `bsr` they work for 0, which gives 64 and sets the carry
  flag; the zero flag says the result is 0. They need a processor with
  the BMI1 and LZCNT extensions (Intel since 2013, AMD since 2012);
  older ones run them as `bsf` and `bsr` without warning.

---

In the shifts and rotations, the flags are only changed when the count
is not 0, and the overflow flag is only defined for a count of 1.

Flow Control Instructions {#flow-control-instructions}
-------------------------

These instructions may alter the flow of the program.

Table B-4. Flow Control Instructions.

**Instruction** _Operands_ -----> Affected Flags.

---

**call** _Destination address_ -----> none:

> This pushes what would be the next value for _%rip_ (the return
  address) onto the stack, and jumps to the destination address. Used
  for function calls. Alternatively, the destination address can be an
  asterisk followed by a register or a memory location for an indirect
  function call. For example, `call *%rax` will call the function at
  the address in _%rax_. `call printf@PLT` calls a function of a shared
  library through the PLT (see Chapter 8). _%rsp_ must be a multiple
  of 16 when it runs.

**Jcc** _Destination address_ -----> none:

> Conditional branch. `cc` is the *condition code*. Jumps to the given
  address if the condition code is true (set from the previous
  instruction, probably a comparison). Otherwise, goes to the next
  instruction. The condition codes are:

  > - `[n]a[e]` - above (unsigned greater than). An `n` can be added for
        \"not\" and an `e` can be added for \"or equal to\".
    - `[n]b[e]` - below (unsigned less than).
    - `[n]e` - equal to.
    - `[n]z` - zero.
    - `[n]g[e]` - greater than (signed comparison).
    - `[n]l[e]` - less than (signed comparison).
    - `[n]c` - carry flag set.
    - `[n]o` - overflow flag set.
    - `[n]p` - parity flag set.
    - `[n]s` - sign flag set.
    - `rcxz` - _%rcx_ is zero (`jrcxz`).

**jmp** _Destination address_ -----> none:

> An unconditional jump. This simply sets _%rip_ to the destination
  address. Alternatively, the destination address can be an asterisk
  followed by a register for an indirect jump. For example, `jmp *%rax`
  will jump to the address in _%rax_.

**leave** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Ends a stack frame: the same as `movq %rbp, %rsp` followed by
  `popq %rbp`. Compilers put it before `ret`.

**ret** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Pops a value off of the stack and then sets _%rip_ to that value.
  Used to return from function calls.

**syscall** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Calls the kernel: the number of the system call is in _%rax_, and its
  parameters are in _%rdi_, _%rsi_, _%rdx_, _%r10_, _%r8_ and _%r9_. The
  result comes back in _%rax_ (a negative number, `-errno`, means an
  error). It overwrites _%rcx_ and _%r11_ (the processor stores the
  return address and the flags there); the kernel preserves the other
  registers. The 32-bit programs used `int $0x80` instead.

---

Floating-Point Instructions {#floating-point-instructions}
---------------------------

These SSE2 instructions work on the _%xmm0_ to _%xmm15_ registers (see
[Chapter 10](10-counting-like-a-computer.qmd#floating-point-in-assembly-language)).
The `sd` forms work on one `double` (8 bytes), and the `ss` forms on
one `float` (4 bytes).

Table B-5. Floating-Point Instructions.

**Instruction** _Operands_ -----> Affected Flags.

---

**movsd**, **movss** _X/M_, _X/M_ -----> none:

> Copy a `double` or a `float` between memory and an _%xmm_ register
  (X), or between two _%xmm_ registers.

**addsd**, **subsd**, **mulsd**, **divsd** _X/M_, _X_ -----> none:

> Add, subtract, multiply or divide the second operand by the first,
  storing the result in the second. `sqrtsd` computes a square root.
  The `ss` versions work on `float`s.

**cvtsi2sdq** _R/M_, _X_ -----> none:

> Converts a 64-bit integer into a `double`.

**cvttsd2si** _X/M_, _R_ -----> none:

> Converts a `double` into a 64-bit integer, truncating it (dropping
  the part after the point). `cvtss2sd` and `cvtsd2ss` convert between
  `float` and `double`.

**ucomisd** _X/M_, _X_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Compares two `double`s and sets the zero, parity and carry flags like
  an unsigned comparison (use `ja`, `jb`, `jae`, `jbe` after it); it
  clears the overflow, sign and auxiliary carry flags. The parity flag
  is set if one of the numbers is not a number (NaN).

---

String Instructions {#string-instructions}
-------------------

These instructions work on blocks of memory. They use _%rsi_ as the
source address and _%rdi_ as the destination, and after each element
they move both forward by its size (1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, the suffix `b`,
`w`, `l` or `q`), or backwards if the direction flag is 1. The calling
convention guarantees that it is 0 when a function starts.

Table B-6. String Instructions.

**Instruction** _Operands_ -----> Affected Flags.

---

**movsb**, **movsq** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Copy one element from `(%rsi)` to `(%rdi)`. With the `rep` prefix,
  repeat it _%rcx_ times: `rep movsb` copies _%rcx_ bytes, and is how
  `memcpy` copies big blocks on current processors.

**stosb**, **stosq** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Store _%al_ (or _%rax_) at `(%rdi)`. `rep stosb` fills _%rcx_ bytes,
  like `memset`.

**lodsb**, **lodsq** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Load `(%rsi)` into _%al_ (or _%rax_).

**cmpsb**, **cmpsq** _Not Applicable_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Compare `(%rsi)` with `(%rdi)`, like `cmp`. With `repe`, repeat
  while they are equal and _%rcx_ isn\'t 0, which compares two blocks.

**scasb**, **scasq** _Not Applicable_ -----> O/S/Z/A/P/C:

> Compare _%al_ (or _%rax_) with `(%rdi)`. With `repne`, repeat while
  they are different: with _%al_ = 0 and _%rcx_ = -1, `repne scasb`
  finds the end of a string, and the length is `not` _%rcx_ minus 1.

**cld**, **std** _Not Applicable_ -----> D:

> Clear or set the direction flag. A function that sets it must clear
  it before calling another function or returning.

---

Other Instructions {#other-instructions}
------------------

Table B-7. Other Instructions.

**Instruction** _Operands_ -----> Affected Flags.

---

**nop** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Does nothing. Assemblers and compilers use longer forms (up to 15
  bytes) to align code, for example the start of a loop.

**endbr64** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Marks a place where an indirect `call` or `jmp` may land, for CET
  (see
  [Chapter 9](09-intermediate-memory-topics.qmd#chapter-9.-intermediate-memory-topics)).
  On processors without CET it is a `nop`.

**pause** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> A hint for loops that wait for another thread to change a value: it
  saves power and lets the other thread of the same core run.

**rdtsc** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Reads the processor\'s time-stamp counter, which grows at a constant
  rate, into _%rdx_:_%rax_ (the high and the low 32 bits). Programs use
  it to measure short times in cycles.

**cpuid** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Tells which processor this is and what it supports. The question goes
  in _%rax_ (and sometimes _%rcx_), and the answer comes back in _%rax_,
  _%rbx_, _%rcx_ and _%rdx_; for example, `cpuid` with _%rax_ = 7 and
  _%rcx_ = 0 says in bit 3 of _%rbx_ whether BMI1 exists.

**int3** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> A one-byte breakpoint: Linux stops the program with the signal
  `SIGTRAP` (status 133 in the shell). A debugger puts it over the
  instruction where you set a breakpoint.

**ud2** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> An instruction that is guaranteed not to exist: Linux stops the
  program with `SIGILL` (status 132). Compilers put it where the program
  must never arrive.

**hlt** _Not Applicable_ -----> none:

> Stops the processor until the next interrupt. Only the kernel may run
  it; in a user program it is a segmentation fault (status 139), like
  every other privileged instruction.

---

Assembler Directives {#assembler-directives}
--------------------

These are instructions to the assembler and linker, instead of
instructions to the processor. These are used to help the assembler put
your code together properly, and make it easier to use.

Table B-8. Assembler Directives.

**Directive** _Operands_.

---

**.ascii** _Quoted String_:

> Takes the given quoted string and converts it into byte data. Add
  `\0` at the end for a null-terminated string.

**.balign** _Number_:

> Adds bytes until the address is a multiple of the given number, so
  that the data that follows is aligned.

**.byte** _Values_:

> Takes a comma-separated list of values and inserts them right there
  in the program as data.

**.double**, **.float** _Values_:

> Insert floating-point numbers as 8-byte `double`s or 4-byte
  `float`s.

**.endr** _Not Applicable_:

> Ends a repeating section defined with `.rept`.

**.equ** _Label_, _Value_:

> Sets the given label equivalent to the given value. The value can be a
  number, a character, or a constant expression that evaluates to a
  number or character (for example `label_end - label`, or
  `O_WRONLY | O_CREAT`). From that point on, use of the label will be
  substituted for the given value.

**.fill** _Count_, _Size_, _Value_:

> Inserts _Count_ copies of _Value_, each one _Size_ bytes long.
  `.fill 21, 1, 0` reserves 21 bytes of zeros.

**.globl** _Label_:

> Sets the given label as global, meaning that it can be used from
  separately-compiled object files.

**.if** _Expression_, **.error** _Message_, **.endif**:

> Assemble the lines between `.if` and `.endif` only if the expression
  is not 0. With `.error`, the assembler stops with the message; Chapter
  6 uses it to check the size of each record.

**.include** _File_:

> Includes the given file just as if it were typed in right there.

**.lcomm** _Symbol_, _Size_:

> This is used in the `.bss` section to specify storage that should be
  allocated when the program is executed. Defines the symbol with the
  address where the storage will be located, and makes sure that it is
  the given number of bytes long.

**.long** _Values_:

> Takes a sequence of numbers separated by commas, and inserts those
  numbers as 4-byte doublewords right where they are in the program.

**.quad** _Values_:

> Takes a sequence of numbers (or addresses) separated by commas, and
  inserts them as 8-byte quadwords. This is the normal size of the
  numbers in this book.

**.rept** _Count_:

> Repeats everything between this directive and the `.endr` directives
  the number of times specified.

**.section** _Section Name_:

> Switches the section that is being worked on. Common sections include
  `.text` (for code), `.data` (for data embedded in the program
  itself), `.rodata` (for data that is only read), `.bss` (for
  uninitialized global data), `.data.rel.ro` (for tables of addresses
  in PIE programs) and `.note.GNU-stack` (which marks the stack as not
  executable, see Chapter 3).

**.type** _Symbol_, _\@function_:

> Tells the linker that the given symbol is a function.

---

Differences in Other Syntaxes and Terminology {#differences-in-other-syntaxes-and-terminology}
---------------------------------------------

The syntax for assembly language used in this book is known as the
*AT&T* syntax. It is the one supported by the GNU tool chain that comes
standard with every Linux distribution, and the one that `objdump`,
gdb and `rustc --emit asm` use by default. However, the official syntax
for x86-64 assembly language (known as the Intel® syntax) is different.
It is the same assembly language for the same platform, but it looks
different. Some of the differences include:

-   In Intel syntax, the operands of instructions are often reversed.
    The destination operand is listed before the source operand.

-   In Intel syntax, registers are not prefixed with the percent sign
    (`%`).

-   In Intel syntax, a dollar-sign (`$`) is not required to do
    immediate-mode addressing. Instead, non-immediate addressing is
    accomplished by surrounding the address with brackets (`[ ]`).

-   In Intel syntax, the instruction name does not include the size of
    data being moved. If that is ambiguous, it is explicitly stated as
    `BYTE PTR`, `WORD PTR`, `DWORD PTR` or `QWORD PTR` immediately
    after the instruction name.

-   The way that memory addresses are represented in Intel assembly
    language is much different (shown below). An address relative to
    the instruction pointer is written `[rip + label]`.

-   Because the x86 processor line originally started out as a 16-bit
    processor, most literature about x86 processors refer to words as
    16-bit values, call 32-bit values double words and 64-bit values
    quad words. The AT&T suffixes follow the same names (`w`, `l` for
    \"long\", and `q`), and so does the Intel syntax (`WORD`, `DWORD`,
    `QWORD`).

-   Intel assembly language has the ability to address memory as a
    segment/offset pair. We do not mention this because 64-bit Linux
    programs don\'t use segmented memory (except for the `%fs` register,
    which the C library uses for the data of each thread).

Other differences exist, but they are small in comparison. To show some
of the differences, consider the following instructions:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines}
movq $5, %rax
movq 12(%rbx), %rax
movq (%rbx,%rdi), %rcx
movq 8(%rbx,%rdi), %rax
movq (%rbx,%rdi,8), %rax
movq 8(%rbx,%rdi,8), %rax
leaq data(%rip), %rbx
```

In Intel syntax, this would be written as:

```{.nasm .numberLines}
mov  rax, 5
mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbx+12]
mov  rcx, QWORD PTR [rbx+rdi]
mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbx+rdi+8]
mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbx+rdi*8]
mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbx+rdi*8+8]
lea  rbx, [rip+data]
```

The memory reference is a bit easier to read than its AT&T counterpart
because it spells out exactly how the address will be computed. However,
the order of operands in Intel syntax can be confusing. You don\'t need
another tool to read programs in Intel syntax: `objdump -d -M intel`
and gdb\'s `set disassembly-flavor intel` show any program that way,
`rustc` emits it with `-C llvm-args=-x86-asm-syntax=intel`, and the GNU
assembler itself accepts it after the directive
`.intel_syntax noprefix`. This is `003-02-maximum` in both syntaxes
(`objdump -d` and `objdump -d -M intel`, with `--no-show-raw-insn`):


```{.text check=appb-objdump-att}
0000000000401000 <_start>:
  401000:       lea    0xff9(%rip),%rbx        # 402000 <data_items>
  401007:       mov    $0x0,%rcx
  40100e:       mov    (%rbx,%rcx,8),%rax
  401012:       mov    %rax,%rdi

0000000000401015 <_start_loop>:
  401015:       cmp    $0x0,%rax
  401019:       je     40102c <_loop_exit>
  40101b:       inc    %rcx
  40101e:       mov    (%rbx,%rcx,8),%rax
  401022:       cmp    %rdi,%rax
  401025:       jle    401015 <_start_loop>
  401027:       mov    %rax,%rdi
  40102a:       jmp    401015 <_start_loop>
```

```{.text check=appb-objdump-intel}
0000000000401000 <_start>:
  401000:       lea    rbx,[rip+0xff9]        # 402000 <data_items>
  401007:       mov    rcx,0x0
  40100e:       mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbx+rcx*8]
  401012:       mov    rdi,rax

0000000000401015 <_start_loop>:
  401015:       cmp    rax,0x0
  401019:       je     40102c <_loop_exit>
  40101b:       inc    rcx
  40101e:       mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbx+rcx*8]
  401022:       cmp    rax,rdi
  401025:       jle    401015 <_start_loop>
  401027:       mov    rdi,rax
  40102a:       jmp    401015 <_start_loop>
```

Notice that `objdump` leaves out the suffixes (`mov` instead of `movq`)
when the registers already say the size.

Where to Go for More Information {#where-to-go-for-more-information}
--------------------------------

Intel has a set of comprehensive guides to their processors, the
[Intel® 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer\'s
Manuals][AB-Intel-manuals]. Note that all of these use the Intel syntax,
not the AT&T syntax. Volume 2 describes every instruction, with its
exact effect on the flags. AMD publishes the same information for its
processors in the [AMD64 Architecture Programmer\'s Manual][AB-AMD].
Félix Cloutier\'s [x86 and amd64 instruction reference][AB-Cloutier]
has the pages of volume 2 on the web, one per instruction.

In addition, you can find a lot of information in the manual for the
[GNU assembler][AB-GNU-Assembler] (its section on the x86-64
dependent features explains the AT&T syntax and the suffixes).
Similarly, the manual for the [GNU linker][AB-GNU-Linker]. The calling
convention and the formats of the object files are in the
[System V AMD64 psABI][AB-ABI].

[AB-AMD]: https://docs.amd.com/v/u/en-US/40332-PUB_4.08
[AB-Cloutier]: https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/
[AB-GNU-Assembler]: https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/as/index.html
[AB-GNU-Linker]: https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/index.html
[AB-ABI]: https://gitlab.com/x86-psABIs/x86-64-ABI
